claim: Aicardi–Goutières syndrome (AGS) is a severe childhood inflammatory disorder that shows clinical and genetic overlap with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
source: Aicardi–Goutières syndrome (AGS) is a severe childhood inflammatory disorder that shows clinical and genetic overlap with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about AGS that draws from established scientific knowledge about the disease.

claim: AGS is thought to arise from the accumulation of incompletely metabolized endogenous nucleic acid species owing to mutations in nucleic acid-degrading enzymes TREX1 (AGS1), RNase H2 (AGS2, 3 and 4), and SAMHD1 (AGS5).
source: AGS is thought to arise from the accumulation of incompletely metabolized endogenous nucleic acid species owing to mutations in nucleic acid-degrading enzymes TREX1 (AGS1), RNase H2 (AGS2, 3 and 4), and SAMHD1 (AGS5).
evidence: This statement reflects the current scientific understanding of AGS etiology based on prior research.

claim: Fibroblasts from AGS patients with AGS1-5 mutations are burdened by excessive loads of RNA:DNA hybrids.
source: Using genome-wide approaches, we show that fibroblasts from AGS patients with AGS1-5 mutations are burdened by excessive loads of RNA:DNA hybrids.
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq experimental data presented in the manuscript showing accumulation of RNA:DNA hybrids in AGS samples.

claim: AGS fibroblasts display pronounced and global loss of DNA methylation.
source: Using MethylC-seq, we show that AGS fibroblasts display pronounced and global loss of DNA methylation
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq experimental data showing DNA hypomethylation across AGS samples.

claim: AGS-specific RNA:DNA hybrids often occur within DNA hypomethylated regions.
source: demonstrate that AGS-specific RNA:DNA hybrids often occur within DNA hypomethylated regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the overlap analysis between DRIP-seq peaks and DNA methylation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AGS is a severe inflammatory encephalopathy characterized by neurological dysfunction, psychomotor retardation, seizures, unexplained fevers, joint stiffness, basal ganglia calcification, and chilblain skin lesions.
source: Aicardi–Goutières syndrome (AGS) is a severe inflammatory encephalopathy characterized by neurological dysfunction, psychomotor retardation, seizures, unexplained fevers, joint stiffness, basal ganglia calcification, and chilblain skin lesions (Rice et al., 2007b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature describing AGS clinical features.

claim: Both AGS and SLE are characterized and driven by excessive expression of interferon alpha.
source: Both diseases are characterized, and to a large extent driven, by excessive expression of interferon alpha, a potent anti-viral cytokine associated with heightened innate immune response and inflammation (Crow, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on AGS and SLE pathology.

claim: AGS is a monogenic disorder caused by mutations in any one of the six AGS genes.
source: AGS is a monogenic disorder caused by mutations in any one of the six AGS genes.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the genetic basis of AGS.

claim: The AGS genes encode for TREX1 (AGS1), RNase H2 subunits (AGS2, 3, and 4), SAMHD1 (AGS5), and ADAR1 (AGS6).
source: The AGS genes encode for the 3′ to 5′ single-stranded DNA exonuclease TREX1 (AGS1) (Crow et al., 2006a), the RNA:DNA hybrid-specific ribonuclease H2 subunits (RNase H2A, B and C, corresponding to AGS4, 2 and 3, respectively) (Crow et al., 2006b), the 3′ to 5′ exonuclease and dNTP hydrolase SAMHD1 (AGS5) (Rice et al., 2009; Goldstone et al., 2011), and the RNA adenosine deaminase ADAR1 (AGS6) (Rice et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature identifying AGS genes.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in the cytosolic double-stranded RNA receptor gene IFIH1 have been shown to be associated with AGS.
source: Recently, gain-of-function mutations in the cytosolic double-stranded RNA receptor gene IFIH1 have also been shown to be associated with AGS (Rice et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on IFIH1 mutations in AGS.

claim: Mutations in TREX1 and the RNASEH2 genes have been implicated in SLE.
source: Interestingly, mutations in TREX1 and the RNASEH2 genes have also been implicated in SLE, further illustrating the genetic link between AGS and SLE (Lee-Kirsch et al., 2007; Gunther et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on genetic links between AGS and SLE.

claim: DNA hypomethylation triggers increased B cell autoreactivity and the development of drug-induced and idiopathic human lupus.
source: Characterizing putative epigenetic deregulation in AGS is all the more justified given that DNA hypomethylation, either spontaneous or caused by drug exposure, triggers increased B cell autoreactivity and the development of drug-induced and idiopathic human lupus (Richardson, 1986; Quddus et al., 1993; Yung et al., 1995; Jeffries et al., 2011; Absher et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature on DNA hypomethylation in lupus.

claim: Loss of DNA methylation, albeit modest and restricted to specific autoimmunity-related genes, was reported in SLE patients.
source: Furthermore, loss of DNA methylation, albeit modest and restricted to specific autoimmunity-related genes, was reported in SLE patients (Richardson et al., 1990; Ballestar et al., 2006; Javierre et al., 2010; Jeffries et al., 2011; Absher et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature on DNA methylation in SLE.

claim: AGS fibroblasts are characterized by an activated antiviral, immune response with a characteristic interferon signature.
source: Transcriptional profiling via RNA-seq showed that AGS fibroblasts are characterized by an activated antiviral, immune response with a characteristic interferon signature.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript showing upregulation of immune and interferon-related genes.

claim: A total of 98 and 209 genes were significantly up- and down-regulated, respectively, in at least one AGS sample.
source: We identified a total of 98 and 209 genes that were significantly up- and down-regulated, respectively, in at least one AGS sample (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis and referenced figures showing differential gene expression.

claim: AGS down-regulated genes significantly associated with ontologies linked to cell adhesion and the extracellular matrix.
source: AGS down-regulated genes significantly associated with ontologies linked to cell adhesion and the extracellular matrix (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Genes involved in inflammation, immune responses, chemokine signaling pathways, and sensing of viral nucleic acids were up-regulated in AGS patient cells.
source: Genes involved in inflammation, immune responses, chemokine signaling pathways, and sensing of viral nucleic acids were up-regulated in AGS patient cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing upregulation of immune-related genes.

claim: Genes for the major pro-inflammatory cytokine IL1β and the CXCL5 and CXCL6 chemokines were up-regulated in several AGS patients.
source: Genes for the major pro-inflammatory cytokine IL1β (Zhao et al., 2013b) and the CXCL5 and CXCL6 chemokines were up-regulated in several AGS patients (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and referenced figures showing gene expression changes.

claim: Genes involved in anti-viral responses (RSAD2, OASL, IGF2BP1, BST2), in particular interferon-inducible genes, were up-regulated in multiple AGS samples.
source: Genes involved in anti-viral responses (RSAD2, OASL, IGF2BP1, BST2), in particular interferon-inducible genes, were also up-regulated in multiple AGS samples (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data and referenced figures showing upregulation of antiviral genes.

claim: RNase H2 generally degrades RNA:DNA hybrids.
source: RNase H2 generally degrades RNA:DNA hybrids (Cerritelli and Crouch, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on RNase H2 function.

claim: RNase H2 is specifically responsible for removing single ribonucleotides that are misincorporated during DNA replication.
source: and is specifically responsible for removing single ribonucleotides that are misincorporated during DNA replication (Reijns et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on RNase H2 function.

claim: Cells from two patients mutated in RNASEH2B (AGS2) showed a twofold to threefold increase in ribonucleotide labeling.
source: Cells from two patients mutated in RNASEH2B (AGS2) showed a twofold to threefold increase in labeling (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nick translation assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cells from two patients mutated in the catalytic RNase H2A subunit (AGS4) showed a pronounced 10–25-fold increase in ribonucleotides.
source: Cells from two patients mutated in the catalytic RNase H2A subunit (AGS4) showed a pronounced 10–25-fold increase in ribonucleotides (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nick translation assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: No significant increase in ribonucleotide loads could be detected in patients mutated in TREX1 (AGS1) or SAMHD1 (AGS5).
source: By contrast, no significant increase in ribonucleotide loads could be detected in patients mutated in TREX1 (AGS1) or SAMHD1 (AGS5) (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nick translation assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: AGS and control fibroblasts share a total of 15,897 DRIP peaks representing approximately 141 megabases of genomic space.
source: DRIP-seq revealed that AGS and control fibroblasts share a total of 15,897 DRIP peaks representing approximately 141 megabases of genomic space (Figure 3A,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis and referenced figures.

claim: 32% of common DRIP peaks mapped to promoters or gene ends, which represents a strong enrichment over expected genomic distribution.
source: Consistent with prior studies, 32% of these peaks mapped to promoters or gene ends, which represents a strong enrichment over expected genomic distribution and further indicates that gene ends correspond to R-loop formation hotspots (Ginno et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis and comparison to prior studies.

claim: 56% of the R-loop signal mapped onto gene bodies.
source: Our high-coverage DRIP-seq data also revealed that 56% of the R-loop signal mapped onto gene bodies, suggesting that RNA–DNA entanglements during transcription are prevalent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Only 15.6% of common R-loop peaks mapped to intergenic regions.
source: By contrast, only 15.6% of common R-loop peaks mapped to intergenic regions, consistent with a predominant genic origin for R-loop formation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Common DRIP peaks showed strong overlap with GC skew.
source: Overall, common DRIP peaks showed strong overlap with GC skew (Figure 3B), a key sequence determinant that favors co-transcriptional R-loop formation (Ginno et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis and a citation to prior literature on GC skew and R-loops.

claim: A large excess of DRIP peaks (33,781 in total) was observed specifically in AGS cells.
source: Despite the relative agreement between AGS and control R-loop profiles over a broad set of common peaks, a large excess of DRIP peaks (33,781 in total) was observed specifically in AGS cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AGS-specific DRIP peaks in each AGS subtype were both threefold to fourfold greater in numbers and occupied a three to four times larger genomic space than control-specific peaks.
source: While a small number of DRIP peaks were also unique to the control sample, AGS-specific DRIP peaks in each AGS subtype were both threefold to fourfold greater in numbers, and when combined, occupied a three to four times larger genomic space than control-specific peaks (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: On average, AGS-specific DRIP peaks occupied an additional 23.8 megabases of DNA sequence.
source: On average, AGS-specific DRIP peaks occupied an additional 23.8 megabases of DNA sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis.

claim: AGS-specific DRIP peaks were threefold to sevenfold less likely to overlap with GC skew than common DRIP peaks.
source: Unlike common DRIP peaks, AGS-specific DRIP peaks were threefold to sevenfold less likely to overlap with GC skew (Figure 3B), suggesting that they may originate according to a non-canonical mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis and includes an inference about mechanism.

claim: AGS-specific DRIP peaks were depleted at transcription start sites (TSSs) and transcription termination sites (TTSs).
source: Additionally, AGS-specific DRIP peaks were depleted at transcription start sites (TSSs) and transcription termination sites (TTSs) (Figure 3D), where R-loops are typically observed (Ginno et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3D and comparison to prior literature.

claim: AGS2- and AGS4-specific peaks were significantly enriched over intergenic portions of the human genome.
source: In contrast, AGS2- and AGS4-specific peaks were significantly enriched over intergenic portions of the human genome (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: AGS1- and AGS5-specific DRIP peaks were enriched over gene body regions.
source: AGS1- and AGS5-specific DRIP peaks were instead enriched over gene body regions (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: All AGS-specific DRIP peaks were significantly enriched in repeat classes corresponding to long interspersed nuclear elements (LINE) and long terminal repeats (LTR) retrotransposons.
source: Interestingly, all AGS-specific DRIP peaks were significantly enriched in repeat classes corresponding to long interspersed nuclear elements (LINE) and long terminal repeats (LTR) retrotransposons (Figure 3D,F,G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by DRIP-seq data analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: All AGS cells displayed significant, global, DNA hypomethylation.
source: All AGS cells displayed significant, global, DNA hypomethylation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: AGS2 and 4 cells showed profound DNA hypomethylation, with a ∼20% reduction in genomic methylation levels overall.
source: AGS2 and 4 cells showed profound DNA hypomethylation, with a ∼20% reduction in genomic methylation levels overall.
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data analysis.

claim: AGS1 and 5 showed a more moderate, but still highly significant, 5–10% reduction in DNA methylation.
source: AGS1 and 5 showed a more moderate, but still highly significant, 5–10% reduction in DNA methylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data analysis.

claim: The reduction in DNA methylation affected TSSs and TTSs and spread along the lengths of entire chromosomes.
source: This reduction affected TSSs and TTSs (Figure 4B,C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and spread along the lengths of entire chromosomes (Figure 4D), significantly impacting nearly all genomic compartments, including genic, intergenic, and repeat regions (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: LINE and LTR elements were significantly hypomethylated in all AGS subtypes.
source: Analysis of repeat classes further revealed that LINE and LTR elements were significantly hypomethylated in all AGS subtypes (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Pyrosequencing assays targeting human-specific LINE-1 elements revealed a small but significant decrease in DNA methylation over 4 CpG sites carried at the LINE-1 5′-UTR promoter.
source: Pyrosequencing assays targeting human-specific LINE-1 elements also revealed a small but significant decrease in DNA methylation over 4 CpG sites carried at the LINE-1 5′-UTR promoter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pyrosequencing data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: SINE elements, satellite repeats, and other repeat types were significantly hypomethylated in AGS2 and 4 but not always in AGS1 and 5.
source: SINE elements, satellite repeats, and other repeat types were significantly hypomethylated in AGS2 and 4 but not always in AGS1 and 5 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The profound reduction in DNA methylation was not caused by any detectable deregulation in the expression of genes encoding for the DNA methylation machinery or of components of a putative DNA de-methylation system.
source: This profound reduction in DNA methylation was not caused by any detectable deregulation in the expression of genes encoding for the DNA methylation machinery or of components of a putative DNA de-methylation system (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in the referenced figure.

claim: PMDs in control fibroblasts were generally shared by AGS fibroblasts but not by embryonic stem (ES) cells.
source: PMDs in control fibroblasts were generally shared by AGS fibroblasts but not by embryonic stem (ES) cells (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), consistent with the notion that they represent fibroblast-specific PMDs.
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data analysis shown in the referenced figures and includes an inference about cell-type specificity.

claim: AGS2 and AGS4 fibroblasts displayed broader PMDs than the control cells.
source: AGS2 and AGS4 fibroblasts displayed broader PMDs than the control cells, while the size of PMD regions in AGS1 and AGS5 cells was relatively unchanged (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Common PMDs resided within silenced genomic regions enriched for Lamin-B1 and the silencing mark histone H3 Lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3).
source: Analysis of the chromatin features associated with PMDs showed that common PMDs resided within silenced genomic regions enriched for Lamin-B1, a component of the nuclear lamina, and the silencing mark histone H3 Lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3), as described previously (Berman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of chromatin features overlapping with PMDs and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Common PMDs were strongly depleted for the H3K27me3 mark.
source: Common PMDs were also strongly depleted for the H3K27me3 mark, a modification associated with facultative heterochromatin and silencing over developmental genes (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of chromatin features shown in the referenced figures.

claim: AGS-specific PMDs, while still associated with Lamin-B1 and to some extent with H3K9me3, were enriched for H3K27me3, particularly over regions corresponding normally to large H3K27me3 blocks.
source: Interestingly, AGS-specific PMDs, while still associated with Lamin-B1 and to some extent with H3K9me3, were enriched for H3K27me3, particularly over regions corresponding normally to large H3K27me3 blocks (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of chromatin features shown in the referenced figures.

claim: In AGS1 and AGS5 fibroblasts, DRIP peaks, whether common or AGS-unique, mostly landed in HMD regions.
source: In AGS1 and AGS5 fibroblasts, which showed only moderate DNA hypomethylation and limited additional PMDs, DRIP peaks, whether common or AGS-unique, mostly landed in HMD regions (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis between DRIP-seq and methylation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Nearly half of the AGS-unique DRIP peaks in AGS2 and AGS4 fibroblasts landed on PMD regions while only 10–15% of common DRIP peaks matched to PMDs in these two samples.
source: In sharp contrast, nearly half of the AGS-unique DRIP peaks in AGS2 and AGS4 fibroblasts landed on PMD regions while only 10–15% of common DRIP peaks matched to PMDs in these two samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis between DRIP-seq and methylation data.

claim: Two-thirds of PMD-contained AGS-unique DRIP peaks matched to AGS-specific PMDs.
source: Furthermore, two-thirds of these PMD-contained AGS-unique DRIP peaks matched to AGS-specific PMDs (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The DNA methylation levels measured over AGS1-, AGS2-, and AGS4- (but not AGS5) unique DRIP peaks were significantly lower in their own respective samples compared to the DNA methylation levels of that same regions measured in control.
source: Consistent with this, the DNA methylation levels measured over AGS1-, AGS2-, and AGS4- (but not AGS5) unique DRIP peaks were significantly lower in their own respective samples compared to the DNA methylation levels of that same regions measured in control (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by methylation analysis of DRIP peak regions shown in Figure 5F.

claim: RNASEH2A KO cells showed higher levels of gamma H2AX, indicative of an activated DNA damage signaling.
source: As expected from previous reports (Reijns et al., 2012; Gunther et al., 2015), we observed higher levels of gamma H2AX in RNASEH2A KO cells (Figure 6B), indicative of an activated DNA damage signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 6B and citations to prior literature.

claim: Knockout of the RNASEH2A gene triggers the reactivation of the silent GFP reporter in HeLa-GFP cells.
source: Compared to scramble, RNASEH2A KO cells showed a clear increase in the number and brightness of GFP-positive cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: GFP expression in RNASEH2A KO cells was 14-fold higher than in scramble cells.
source: GFP expression in RNASEH2A KO cells was 14-fold higher than in scramble cells, as measured by Western blot (Figure 6D), demonstrating reactivation of the GFP reporter gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: RNASEH2A KO cells showed significant DNA hypomethylation relative to scramble at two 5′-UTR portions common to LINE-1 elements.
source: RNASEH2A KO cells showed significant DNA hypomethylation relative to scramble (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: RNASEH2A deficiency has a direct effect in triggering DNA hypomethylation and gene reactivation at least for the loci studied.
source: This suggests a direct effect of RNASEH2A deficiency in triggering DNA hypomethylation and gene reactivation at least for the loci studied here.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the CRISPR knockout experiments showing DNA hypomethylation and GFP reactivation.

claim: The DNA hypomethylation reported in AGS is stronger than that previously reported in SLE.
source: While additional samples encompassing other AGS mutations subtypes will need to be studied to confirm this trend, this observation nonetheless reinforces the similarities between AGS and SLE, although the DNA hypomethylation reported here is stronger than that previously reported in SLE.
evidence: This claim compares the magnitude of DNA hypomethylation observed in this study to prior reports in SLE.

claim: In AGS2 and AGS4, the DNA hypomethylation led to the formation of AGS-specific PMDs in addition to those normally observed in fibroblasts.
source: In AGS2 and AGS4, where the effect was most marked, the DNA hypomethylation led to the formation of AGS-specific PMDs in addition to those normally observed in fibroblasts (Lister et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by MethylC-seq data analysis and a citation to prior literature on fibroblast PMDs.

claim: AGS-specific PMDs, but not common PMDs, were enriched over regions marked by H3K27me3, a mark of facultative heterochromatin associated with developmental silencing.
source: Interestingly, AGS-specific PMDs, but not common PMDs, were also enriched over regions marked by H3K27me3, a mark of facultative heterochromatin associated with developmental silencing (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by chromatin feature analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Silent, condensed genomic regions may be intrinsically prone to becoming PMDs, and this tendency is made worse by AGS2 and AGS4 mutations.
source: This suggests that silent, condensed genomic regions, may in fact be intrinsically prone to becoming PMDs, and that this tendency is made worse by AGS2 and AGS4 mutations.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that AGS-specific PMDs overlap with silenced chromatin regions.

claim: Defects in TREX1, RNase H2, and SAMHD1 all trigger the DNA damage response and are associated with increased genomic instability.
source: While the precise mechanism responsible for DNA hypomethylation in AGS remains to be elucidated, it is worth noting that defects in TREX1, RNase H2, and SAMHD1 all trigger the DNA damage response and are associated with increased genomic instability (Yang et al., 2007; Reijns et al., 2012; Clifford et al., 2014; Kretschmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature on DNA damage in AGS.

claim: RNase H2 associates with the DNA replication fork through the PCNA (proliferating cell nuclear antigen) clamp.
source: RNase H2 in fact associates with the DNA replication fork through the PCNA (proliferating cell nuclear antigen) clamp (Bubeck et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on RNase H2 function.

claim: TREX1 was found to translocate to the nucleus upon replication stress where it might be involved in processing aberrant DNA replication intermediates.
source: and TREX1 was found to translocate to the nucleus upon replication stress where it might be involved in processing aberrant DNA replication intermediates (Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on TREX1 function.

claim: The replication stress caused by AGS mutations may indirectly result in defects in replication-coupled, DNMT1-mediated DNA methylation maintenance.
source: It is therefore possible that the replication stress caused by AGS mutations indirectly results in defects in replication-coupled, DNMT1-mediated DNA methylation maintenance (Figure 7) (Law and Jacobsen, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic proposal based on known connections between replication and DNA methylation maintenance.

claim: The PCNA clamp unloads from the lagging strand of stalled DNA replication forks.
source: In support of this notion, a recent report shows that the PCNA clamp unloads from the lagging strand of stalled DNA replication forks (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on PCNA behavior at stalled forks.

claim: The DNMT1 maintenance DNA methyltransferase binds to PCNA.
source: Given that the DNMT1 maintenance DNA methyltransferase binds to PCNA (Leonhardt et al., 1992)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on DNMT1-PCNA interaction.

claim: DNMT1 requires PCNA binding for efficient activity.
source: and requires PCNA binding for efficient activity (Schermelleh et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on DNMT1 function.

claim: Replication stress may lead to inefficient DNA methylation maintenance, particularly in silent, compact regions of the genome such as heterochromatic regions.
source: it is plausible that replication stress may lead to inefficient DNA methylation maintenance, particularly in silent, compact regions of the genome such as heterochromatic regions.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic proposal connecting replication stress to DNA hypomethylation.

claim: 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine causes genome-wide DNA damage.
source: Interestingly, 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine, a drug best known as a DNA-demethylating agent, in fact causes genome-wide DNA damage (Karpf et al., 1999; Palii et al., 2008; Orta et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature on 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine effects.

claim: Pronounced DNA hypomethylation causes genomic instability.
source: Finally, pronounced DNA hypomethylation is also known to cause genomic instability (Jackson-Grusby et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2007; Liao et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature on DNA hypomethylation and genomic instability.

claim: There may be a positive feedback loop that links and amplifies defects in DNA replication stress and DNA hypomethylation pathways.
source: suggesting a possible positive feedback loop that may link and amplify defects in either pathways (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about a feedback mechanism based on the bidirectional relationship between DNA damage and hypomethylation.

claim: RNA-seq characterization only identified a modest number of up- and down-regulated genes that were enriched for ontologies reflecting the biology of the disease itself, such as immunomodulatory genes.
source: However, our RNA-seq characterization only identified a modest number of up- and down-regulated genes that were enriched for ontologies reflecting the biology of the disease itself, such as immunomodulatory genes (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: There is no evidence for a global alteration of transcriptional profiles as a result of the DNA hypomethylation in AGS.
source: There is therefore no evidence for a global alteration of transcriptional profiles as a result of the DNA hypomethylation in AGS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data showing limited transcriptional changes.

claim: There is a general absence of direct connections between DNA hypomethylation and gene reactivation.
source: This is consistent with the general absence of direct connections between DNA hypomethylation and gene reactivation (Bestor et al., 2015), including in extremely hypomethylated mouse ES cells (Li et al., 1992; Tsumura et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on DNA methylation and gene expression.

claim: DNA methylation is the primary silencing force ensuring retrotransposon control in somatic cells.
source: DNA methylation is indeed the primary silencing force ensuring retrotransposon control in somatic cells (Walsh et al., 1998; Yoder and Bestor, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on DNA methylation and transposon silencing.

claim: The cGAS-STING pathway activates the interferon response upon sensing of cytosolic DNA and RNA:DNA hybrids.
source: The cGAS-STING pathway activates the interferon response upon sensing of not only cytosolic DNA (Sun et al., 2013), but also RNA:DNA hybrids (Mankan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on cGAS-STING pathway.

claim: Multiple dsDNA break repair proteins can sense damaged DNA and induce a STING-mediated type I IFN response.
source: Interestingly, several studies reported that multiple dsDNA break repair proteins can sense damaged DNA and induce a STING-mediated type I IFN response (Zhang et al., 2011; Kondo et al., 2013; Hartlova et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on DNA damage sensing and interferon response.

claim: The endosomal receptor TLR9 has been identified as an RNA:DNA hybrid sensor in addition to its canonical role in sensing unmethylated CpG-rich DNA.
source: Besides STING, it is worth noting that the endosomal receptor TLR9 has also been identified as an RNA:DNA hybrid sensor (Rigby et al., 2014) in addition to its canonical role in sensing unmethylated CpG-rich DNA (Hemmi et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on TLR9 function.

claim: AGS mutations-induced DNA hypomethylation may contribute to the increased interferon response in AGS.
source: It is therefore possible that AGS mutations-induced DNA hypomethylation also contributes to the increased interferon response in AGS (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about how DNA hypomethylation might contribute to interferon response.

claim: Treatment of colon adenocarcinoma with 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine triggers a prominent interferon response.
source: Interestingly, treatment of colon adenocarcinoma with 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine, which causes DNA damage and DNA demethylation, triggers a prominent interferon response (Karpf et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine effects.

claim: R-loops are long RNA:DNA hybrid structures that form co-transcriptionally upon re-annealing of the RNA transcript to the template DNA strand, forcing the non-template strand into a single-stranded state.

evidence: This is a definitional statement about R-loops based on established knowledge.

claim: R-loops are enriched at the 5′- and 3′-ends of human genes where they play roles in epigenetic control and transcription regulation.
source: R-loops are enriched at the 5′- and 3′-ends of human genes where they play roles in epigenetic control and transcription regulation (Ginno et al., 2012, 2013).

claim: RNA transcripts may serve as a template for the repair of double-strand DNA breaks upon hybridization to DNA via Rad52.
source: It was recently described that RNA transcripts may serve as a template for the repair of double-strand DNA breaks upon hybridization to DNA via Rad52, a key member of the homologous recombination pathway.
evidence: This claim reflects recent findings in the literature about RNA-templated DNA repair.

source: Interestingly, RNase H2 activity was shown to block the formation of these RNA:DNA hybrids (Keskin et al., 2014).

source: It is therefore possible that some of the DNA breaks caused by AGS mutations and replication stress are repaired according to a pathway prone to RNA:DNA hybrid formation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic proposal about how RNA:DNA hybrids might form during DNA repair in AGS.

claim: Regions experiencing DNA hypomethylation as a result of AGS mutations may undergo spurious transcription that leads to co-transcriptional R-loop formation.

claim: AGS fibroblasts exhibit an activated immune, inflammatory, and anti-viral state.

claim: AGS-specific RNA:DNA hybrids may originate according to a non-canonical mechanism.
source: Unlike common DRIP peaks, AGS-specific DRIP peaks were threefold to sevenfold less likely to overlap with GC skew (Figure 3B), suggesting that they may originate according to a non-canonical mechanism.

claim: AGS mutations in TREX1, RNASEH2A, RNASEH2B, and SAMHD1 are associated with the accumulation of RNA:DNA hybrids over repeat-rich intergenic and gene body regions.

evidence: This is a summary inference based on the DRIP-seq data analysis.

claim: The two main features observed in AGS samples, excessive RNA:DNA hybrid formation and DNA hypomethylation, often overlap.
source: Thus, our data show a remarkable agreement between regions that accumulate RNA:DNA hybrids in the AGS2, AGS4, and to a lesser extent AGS1 subtypes and regions that undergo DNA hypomethylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap analysis between DRIP-seq and methylation data.

claim: TREX1, RNase H2, and SAMHD1 mutations share common molecular abnormalities including genome-wide DNA hypomethylation and accumulation of RNA:DNA hybrid species.
source: Our data therefore provide the first evidence that TREX1, RNASEH2, and SAMHD1 mutations share common molecular abnormalities including genome-wide DNA hypomethylation and accumulation of RNA:DNA hybrid species.

claim: This study provides the first evidence of epigenetic perturbations in AGS.
source: Altogether, our data suggest that RNA:DNA hybrids may represent a common immunogenic form of nucleic acids in AGS and provide the first evidence of epigenetic perturbations in AGS, furthering the links between AGS and SLE.
evidence: This claim is based on the novel DNA methylation findings presented in the manuscript.
